Making eye contact with other people
Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation

I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me

Memory.value: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns
The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over

What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it
I am not sure my life is worth living anymore

issues.item: Triggers: Pregnancy/Birth Reminders: Pregnancy, childbirth, or babies in general
issues.explanation: Pregnancy/birth reminders are hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma of physical abuse by a romantic partner in this 34-year-old male unless there is unreported trauma content involving pregnancy, childbirth, or infants. The other trigger items point toward sexualized/interpersonal threat and hospital-associated reminders, making this item the clearest trauma-incongruent outlier.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Checking Locks: repeatedly check locks, doors, or windows
issues.explanation: Repeated lock-checking is more suggestive of fear of external intrusion/burglary than trauma-specific coping with partner physical abuse, and it is weakly connected to the rest of the profile. The other maladaptive strategies reflect interpersonal avoidance and affect suppression, whereas this item introduces a different safety concern.

issues.item: Threat: Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
issues.explanation: This threat item duplicates compulsive checking behavior rather than describing a perceived current threat state, and it implies fear of break-in/external danger that is not otherwise supported by the trauma narrative, appraisals, or memory content. In combination with the matching maladaptive strategy item, it forms an internally coherent pair but one that is poorly integrated with the rest of the formulation.

vignette: Three years ago, the altercation with his partner escalated when a bottle shattered against the kitchen tile. Before Elijah could retreat, his partner's hands closed around his throat, and a heavy force drove him to the hardwood floor. The violence was relentless, but what seared into Elijah's memory most was the way his partner's eyes tracked him during the assault with a look that felt distinctly sexual, treating him as an object to be controlled. When a neighbor called for help, the ride to the trauma center carried the sharp, clinical scent of antiseptic that still clings to his memory. He was left alone with a male intake nurse who stood in the doorway, his gaze lingering on Elijah's bruised body with the same detached scrutiny. That combination of the sterile smell, the heavy silence, and the male presence watching him without empathy became the blueprint of the assault. When the memories surface, they do not arrive as recollections. They collapse the years into the present. Sometimes Elijah hears his partner's low, rhythmic warnings echoing in the quiet of his own apartment, and the copper taste of a bitten lip floods his mouth, tasting exactly as it did on the floorboards. He cannot distinguish the then from the now; his shoulders lock, his breath shallows, and his body sits coiled, braced for impact. He scans every room he enters, tracking the arc of a stranger's neck or the positioning of a colleague's hands. He watches people closely, reading micro-expressions for the flicker of aggression, convinced that the environment is inherently unpredictable. Alongside the constant alarm, Elijah constructed a routine of withdrawal. He learned to flatten his own joy, pushing away moments of laughter or relief because warmth felt fundamentally unsafe. When he looked at his partner or coworkers, his eyes dropped immediately to the floor or the desk surface; meeting a gaze felt intrusive and overwhelming. He stopped engaging in any necessary debates. If a parolee pushed back on a curfew violation, Elijah would back down or defer the discussion, his throat tight at the prospect of disagreement. Over months, this became his pattern. At work, his caseload grew heavier as supervisors noted his reluctance to confront behavioral violations. He began leaving early on days he knew involved field interviews, choosing patrol routes that kept him away from male-dominated stations. His avoidance of male supervisors meant he stopped attending mandatory training, further isolating him from the precinct floor. In his relationship, the habit of pushing away positive emotions left his partner confused by the sudden emotional distance, even as Elijah desperately wanted closeness. The distance between Elijah and his life grew wider. He looked at the empty side of his bed, the paused promotion, the silent phone, and concluded that his life had been dismantled beyond repair. When he tried to report the initial assault to the authorities, he was told there was insufficient evidence, a dismissal that cemented his conviction that what happened to him was profoundly unjust and that the system had abandoned him. The weight of that abandonment, combined with the relentless tension in his muscles and the unyielding fear that the next moment would bring the same violation, left him wondering if his existence held any value at all. He sought help last Tuesday after his partner found him sitting in the parked cruiser outside the precinct, his knuckles white on the steering wheel, unable to bring himself to go in for his shift. What frightened him most was not the flashbacks or the flinching at antiseptic wipes in the breakroom, but the certainty that he was slipping away from the person he used to be. He sat in the intake chair now, his eyes fixed on the grain of the wood table, hoping someone might show him how to unclench a life that felt permanently broken, and dreading the day he would have to look anyone in the eye again.
